1.pericope_label: Nebuchadnezzar makes Jehoiakim his servant three years; he rebels, bands are sent against Judah, he dies, and Egypt comes out no more

schools.summary: Gill dates the subjugation to the latter end of the third or the beginning of the fourth year, has Jehoiakim taken and restored on promise of obedience with Daniel and his companions carried off as hostages along with temple vessels, reads the captivity as a sure decree for which God stirred up Nebuchadnezzar, and has the king die at the gates as soon as he came out, unburied, with the vessels lodged in the idol house at Babylon.

Henry reads the revolt as folly on both counts, that serving God would have spared the servitude and keeping his word would have left his condition no worse, notices that the bands are given no commission from Nebuchadnezzar but only from the King of kings, and finds two intentions in the judgment, the punishment of Manasseh after long waiting for a repentance that never came and the fulfilling of the prophecies, with the penalty remitted only as to its temporal side since national sins lie charged on the land.

Clarke supplies the political frame, Nebuchadnezzar sent by his father against revolted provinces and taking all Egypt held from the Euphrates to the Nile, points back to Huldah for the word fulfilled, and will scarcely reckon the three months of Jehoiachin a reign at all; Wesley makes the sins properly Judah own, Manasseh only as they repeated them.

Ellicott dates the invasion from Carchemish and the death of Nabopolassar, traces the revolt to Egyptian instigation and the raiders to hereditary enemies taking reprisals for Josiah power over them, renders the clause strictly as only upon the mouth of Jehovah, refuses to let the charge be softened into mere persistence in Manasseh kind of sin, and reads the withheld burial notice as significant; Delitzsch treats the third year as no more than the extreme terminus from which to count and finds the received reconciliation of the burial notice with Jeremiah insufficient.

debates.question: When did Nebuchadnezzar first subdue Jehoiakim?

sides.position: in the fifth or sixth year, after Carchemish in the fourth and the recall to Babylon on Nabopolassar death
the third year is only the extreme terminus from which to count; Carchemish fell early in the fourth year and Jerusalem was taken in the same year
at the latter end of the third or the beginning of the fourth year, when Jehoiakim was taken and restored on promise of obedience

debates.question: On what ground did the judgment fall?

sides.position: on the sins of Manasseh, visited after long waiting, with the innocent blood singled out as unpardoned and the prophecies to be fulfilled
the blood cried to heaven, and children suffering for their fathers was precisely the Old Testament doctrine until Ezekiel proclaimed another
the measure of sins was full, so that no intercession, even of Moses and Samuel, would have availed
properly for their own sins, and for Manasseh only as they made his sins their own by repeating them

debates.question: How did Jehoiakim come to his end?

sides.position: he fell in an encounter with the freebooters and his body was left where it lay; the words imply no peaceful death
he died at the gates as soon as he came out of Jerusalem and had no burial at all
the statement no longer contradicts Jeremiah, as is generally admitted, but the received solution is insufficient

outliers: Clarke alone measures the conquest from the Euphrates to the Nile and makes Nebuchadnezzar his father deputy against the revolted provinces.
Ellicott alone glosses out of his sight from the Targum, as the land where God was present in his Temple.
themes: a vassal who kept faith three years
Egypt shut inside its own borders

8.pericope_label: Jehoiachin reigns three months, Jerusalem is besieged, and he goes out to the king of Babylon

schools.summary: Gill reconciles eighteen with eight by a co-regency begun in his father first year, reports a second solution from the eighth year of the captivity, concludes that a copyist very probably wrote eight for eighteen since the Arabic and Syriac read eighteen, makes a partner in the throne a partner in the sins, and says plainly that Nebuchadnezzar came in person following his army.

Henry turns the surrender into a reproach, that the name of Babylon had grown formidable and the king beat a parley, when peace made with God and the method Hezekiah took would have let him hold out with courage and honour, one chasing a thousand, so that wanting the faith and piety of an Israelite he had not the resolution of a man, of a soldier, or of a prince, and he and his house went out prisoners of war as servants of sin do.

Clarke refuses to reconcile the two figures and calls the shorter corrupt, since a king carried to Babylon after three months had wives there and of such an age it could scarcely be said that he did evil as a king, and has him surrender because further defence was useless, hoping for better terms; Wesley takes the co-regency without qualification and adds that the surrender followed the counsel of Jeremiah and was to the king own good.

Ellicott counts the forms of the name and reports the view that the prophet clipped it to foreshadow the fate, weighs and rejects the application of the lion parable to this king, dates the siege to the spring, takes the servants to be generals and reads from the tense that the siege had begun before the king arrived; Delitzsch glosses at that time as the accession or the turn of the year, and has Nebuchadnezzar show none of his earlier favour but treat this king as a rebel.

debates.question: Was Jehoiachin eight or eighteen at his accession?

sides.position: both figures stand, by a co-regency: eight when he began to reign with his father, eighteen when he began to reign alone
the shorter figure is corrupt, since the king had wives at Babylon and could scarcely be said to do evil as a king at that age
the lower number is a slip of the pen

debates.question: Does the parable of the young lion refer to this king?

sides.position: Ewald among others refers it to him
Thenius objects from the brevity of the reign, much of it under siege, and refers it with Hitzig to Zedekiah

debates.question: Why did he go out to the king of Babylon?

sides.position: he despaired of the defence and threw himself on the clemency of Nebuchadnezzar, probably hoping to keep the throne as a vassal
he saw that further defence was useless and hoped for better terms
wanting the faith and piety of an Israelite, he had not the resolution to hold out
the surrender followed the counsel of Jeremiah and was to his own good

outliers: Ellicott alone tracks four or five forms of the king name and passes on the view that the prophet clipped it, leaving a confirming God without the will to confirm.
Delitzsch alone denies that the king mother is named because the king was still a minor.
Ellicott alone records that Josephus called this king naturally good and just, probably on a misreading of Jeremiah.
themes: a reign that was only a captivity
a name clipped to foreshadow a fate
terms sought from a conqueror who gave none
the gate opened instead of defended

13.pericope_label: The treasures and the vessels carried off, ten thousand deported, and Mattaniah made king under the name Zedekiah

schools.summary: Gill has the gates thrown open and the conqueror entering to strip palace and temple alike, limits all Jerusalem to the chief, the honourable, the rich and the useful, gives the seven thousand as the principal men, notes that Jehoiachin remained at Babylon at least thirty-seven years, and makes Mattaniah the third son of Josiah.

Clarke sorts the plundering into three spoliations, under Jehoiakim, here, and under Zedekiah, and gives the figures for the mighty men and the craftsmen; Wesley makes the deported the best and most considerable part, works the arithmetic the same way, observes that smiths could have furnished new arms and fresh trouble, and asks how the golden vessels had survived earlier rifling at all.

Ellicott finds it surprising that anything was left in the treasury, infers secret store-chambers, takes the cutting in pieces as the stripping of gold plate, defines the deported classes against Thenius and Bahr, works out the arithmetic of the ten thousand, and reads the change of name against the prophecy of a king called Jehovah our righteousness; Delitzsch distinguishes the solid-gold vessels taken at the first taking and returned by Cyrus from the plating taken now, and makes Mattaniah the youngest son with the first claim as uncle to a childless youth.

debates.question: How often and how far was the temple spoiled?

sides.position: three times over, under Jehoiakim, at this taking, and finally under Zedekiah
the solid-gold vessels went at the first taking and were given back by Cyrus; what was taken now was the plating
that anything remained after repeated spoliations argues secret store-chambers and supports the account of the sanctuary wealth
the golden vessels survived earlier rifling by the care of priests who hid them, the clemency of conquerors, or a providence disposing their hearts

debates.question: Who were the mighty men, the craftsmen and the smiths?

sides.position: fighting men, with craftsmen workers in wood, stone and metal and smiths properly those who shut, makers of bolts and bars
men of property and artisans rather than warriors
the chief men, the nobles and the artificers, numbered seven thousand and one thousand

debates.question: Where did Mattaniah stand among the sons of Josiah?

sides.position: the third son
the youngest son, who as uncle to a youth too young to have a son fit to reign had the first claim

outliers: Ellicott alone calls the gloss that makes the smiths learned men shutting other mouths with riddles a curiosity of exegesis.
Ellicott alone suspects that setting a native prince on the throne executed a promise made at the surrender.
Delitzsch alone explains why the king, the queen-mother and the wives are held back from the general statement for the later list.
themes: plating stripped from what plunder had spared
a population counted down to its cream
smiths deported so that no arms could be made
a new name that raised false hopes

18.pericope_label: Zedekiah reigns eleven years, does evil in the sight of the LORD, and rebels against the king of Babylon

schools.summary: Gill works back through the three months of Jehoahaz, the eleven years of Jehoiakim and the three months and ten days of his son to fix how old Zedekiah was when Josiah died.

Clarke finds it astonishing that not one of these kings took warning from the judgments which fell on his predecessors, dates the revolt to the eighth year, reproves the breaking of the oath sworn to Babylon and calls it the filling up of the measure of iniquity; Wesley draws the moral backwards, that the sins of the people were the true cause why God gave them wicked kings and suffered them to do wickedly.

Ellicott renders the clause literally and would punctuate so that the rebellion stands on its own, then sets out the diplomacy behind it, the embassy to Pharaoh Hophra, the general rising proposed by the neighbouring peoples, the hopes raised by a prophecy Jeremiah opposed throughout, and the earlier attempts to recover the exiles, concluding that the date of the open revolt cannot be fixed; Delitzsch compares this section with the appendix to Jeremiah and argues that neither text was drawn from the other, and presses that the anger of God made the man king rather than made him wicked.

debates.question: What is the relation between this section and the appendix to the book of Jeremiah?

sides.position: neither was drawn from the other, since the appendix carries notices on the vessels and the brazen pillars found nowhere in these books

debates.question: Does the anger of the Lord make God the author of Zedekiah wickedness?

sides.position: no; what came to pass by that anger was that such a man became king, and so the cause of the destruction
the raising of such a prince was itself a token of displeasure, his character being able only to hasten the end
the sins of the people were the cause why God gave them wicked kings and suffered them to do wickedly

debates.question: When did the open revolt break out?

sides.position: in the eighth year of his reign
the date cannot be fixed

outliers: Ellicott alone would put a full stop before the last sentence, so that the rebellion is stated on its own and not as what the anger brought about.
Ellicott alone measures the hopes of the revolt by the prophecy of Hananiah and sets Jeremiah against the project throughout.
Delitzsch alone passes on the judgment that Zedekiah was simple and dependent upon his counsellors while despising the word of God.
themes: two texts neither of which copied the other
a wicked king given as a judgment
an alliance canvassed from Egypt to Zidon
an oath sworn by God and broken
